concepts.def: FBI approach (Ressler 1986): classify crime scene as organised or disorganised to infer offender characteristics.
Canter's UK approach: statistical analysis of crime scene data to derive profiles; investigative psychology.
Lombroso's (1876) outdated theory that criminals are evolutionary throwbacks identifiable by physical features.
Criminals score high on extraversion, neuroticism and psychoticism (E, N, P); inherited nervous system underactivity.
Sutherland (1939): criminal behaviour learned from associates whose pro-crime attitudes outweigh anti-crime ones.
Imprisonment aims to deter, rehabilitate, incapacitate and protect; UK recidivism around 48% within one year.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Criminal Psychology — a core area of GCSE Psychology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Criminal Psychology brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Criminal Psychology.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: How are phobias MAINTAINED according to Mowrer's two-process model?
options: Through classical conditioning continuing over time.
Through genetic predisposition.
Because IQ tests are unreliable.
Through operant conditioning - avoidance reduces anxiety (negative reinforcement).

mcqs.q: Why is high IQ a problem for the statistical infrequency definition?
options: 35 percent.
Because IQ tests are unreliable.
It is statistically rare but not abnormal/undesirable.
Because high IQ is actually common.

mcqs.q: In Milgram's study, what percentage of participants gave the maximum 450V shock?
options: 35 percent.
65 percent.
100 percent (all of them).
Through genetic predisposition.
